fact_checks: Nine of the eleven security types declaring 'source' use an optional object described as 'Source code reference', so the claimed sibling pattern is real and dominant.
accesscondition.source is a required string with no description, so the facts do not show whether it means a code reference or something else.
evidence.source is also a required string, but it has an explicit description (origin of an evidence artifact), so a deliberate string-typed 'source' exists and is documented as distinct.
condition, policyrule and validationrule, the types closest to accesscondition, all use the optional source-code-reference object.

arguments_for: Nine sibling types, including condition and policyrule, use an optional source-code-reference object; accesscondition alone deviates without explanation.
The missing description, unlike evidence.source, suggests an accidental typing rather than an intentional distinct meaning.
Required 'source' forces modellers to invent a value for every predicate, even when no code location exists, which hampers CLI validation.
arguments_against: evidence.source shows a required string 'source' can legitimately carry a different meaning.
Accesscondition may intend 'source' as the attribute category (subject, resource, environment), which a code-reference object would break.

arguments_for: The proposed definition names subject claim, resource property and environment value, so 'source' could plausibly be the XACML attribute category for 'field'.
Like evidence.source, accesscondition.source may be a domain attribute that only shares its name with the code reference.
arguments_against: There is no description establishing the alternative meaning, unlike the documented evidence.source.
Accesscondition is embedded in PolicyRule, which uses the code-reference object, so coherence would expect the same.

arguments_for: Whether a predicate carries its own code reference or inherits one from its PolicyRule is a granularity choice for product owners.
One fix renames the string to 'attributeSource' and adds the optional code reference; the other just retypes it. Choosing between them needs a decision.
arguments_against: Required versus optional with an undocumented type looks like an error rather than a deliberate trade-off.
The dominant sibling convention gives a clear default, so little genuine choice remains.

arguments_for: Source-code traceability is arguably a tooling or extraction concern rather than core security semantics.
arguments_against: The attribute is declared in the spec schema itself, so its typing is squarely a spec matter.
The claim concerns schema consistency within the layer, not CLI behaviour.
